Advise
əd-vīz'
v. (to counsel; to give one's judgment on a course of action)
Old French aviser, from Latin ad visum, according to what is seen — to give the judgment one's view supplies. The Hebrew yaats is the standard verb of counsel, from which comes Wonderful, Counsellor.

Biblical Definition

The word enters the histories at the hinge of the divided kingdom. Rehoboam “consulted with the old men, that stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived, and said, How do ye advise that I may answer this people?” (1Ki 12:6). He asked well and then refused the answer: “But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him” (1Ki 12:8), and ten tribes were torn away. Asking for advice is not the same as taking it, and a man who seeks counsel until he finds the counsel he wanted has not sought counsel at all. Proverbs is emphatic on both the necessity and the plurality: “Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established” (Pro 15:22); “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14). The histories also record the danger of a counsellor too much trusted — Ahithophel's advice “was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God” (2Sa 16:23) — and that same counsellor turned traitor. Advice is a gift of God through men, and it is never the oracle.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to advise as to give counsel to; to offer an opinion as worthy or expedient to be followed; and to advise with, to consult and deliberate together.

expand to see more

ADVISE, v.t. [Fr. aviser; ad and visum.] To give counsel to; to offer an opinion, as worthy or expedient to be followed.

I advise thee to the contrary.

2. To give information; to communicate notice; to make acquainted with.

ADVISE, v.i. To deliberate, weigh well, or consider. Advise thyself of what word I shall bring again. 1 Chron. xxi.

Key Scripture

1Ki 12:6 — "And king Rehoboam consulted with the old men, that stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived, and said, How do ye advise that I may answer this people?"

1Ki 12:8 — "But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him, and which stood before him:"

Pro 15:22 — "Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established."

Pro 11:14 — "Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety."

Modern Corruption

Counsel is now sought as confirmation rather than as correction, which is precisely Rehoboam's method and produced precisely his result.

expand to see more

Rehoboam's failure is not that he neglected to ask. He asked twice, and the second asking was the sin. He had a decision already formed and went looking for men who would sign it — men grown up with him, who shared his assumptions and owed him their prospects. Everything about the method looks diligent from outside. The corruption is quiet, common, and it is the ordinary way advice is sought today: a man circulates his plan among those most likely to approve it, calls the approval counsel, and proceeds fortified. Proverbs prescribes a multitude of counsellors precisely because a multitude is harder to select for agreement, and the old men Rehoboam rejected had one qualification the young men lacked — they had stood before Solomon and had watched what heavy yokes cost.

The opposite error is Ahithophel's, and it is the error of the one who receives counsel too well. His advice was esteemed as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God, and that estimate was a snare to David's house long before the man betrayed it. A counsellor is a means, not a mouth of God; where a Christian assigns to a pastor, a mentor, or a gifted friend an authority that belongs only to Scripture, he has made an oracle of a man and will be wounded when the man proves to be one. The Reformed doctrine of the sufficiency of Scripture is not hostile to counsel — the same Bible commands it in the plainest terms — but it fixes counsel in its place: advice is weighed by the word, never above it, and the wisest counsellor in Israel hanged himself when his advice was not taken.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yaats (H3289), to advise or counsel, with etsah (H6098), counsel, and yoets (H3289), a counsellor; Greek sumbouleuo (G4823), to counsel together.

expand to see more

Hebrew yaats (H3289) — to advise, to counsel; how do ye advise that I may answer this people; 1 Kings 12:6.

Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, the thing advised; forsaken by Rehoboam and standing for ever in the LORD; 1 Kings 12:8, Psalm 33:11.

Hebrew yoets — a counsellor; the child born to us is called Wonderful, Counsellor; Isaiah 9:6.

Hebrew sod (H5475) — intimate counsel, a confidential circle; the secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; Psalm 25:14.

Greek sumbouleuo (G4823) — to counsel together, to take counsel with; used both of godly consultation and of the plot against Christ; Matthew 26:4.

Usage

"“How do ye advise that I may answer this people?” — the right question, asked by the wrong heart."

"“He forsook the counsel of the old men” — asking twice until the answer agreed."

"“In the multitude of counsellors there is safety” — a multitude is harder to select for agreement."
